title: Episode 156: Grover Cleveland: The Secret Surgery on the Yacht Oneida and the Pullman Strike
description:
In the summer of 1893, as the Panic of 1893 pushed America toward bankruptcy, President Grover Cleveland discovered a rough, ulcerated tumor on the roof of his mouth. Knowing that disclosure of cancer would panic Wall Street and collapse the gold standard, Cleveland devised the most audacious medical deception in presidential history. Under the guise of a pleasure cruise, six surgeons boarded the yacht Oneida in Long Island Sound and operated on the President inside a rocking cabin, removing his upper left jaw and five teeth entirely through his mouth to avoid leaving a facial scar. Just months later, Cleveland faced down Eugene V. Debs and the massive Pullman Strike, ordering federal troops into Chicago to keep the mails moving. Discover the iron will of Grover Cleveland.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of Grover Cleveland with two of the most gripping crises of his entire career. Hidden beneath the floorboards of a private steam yacht in Long Island Sound, Cleveland underwent a secret, life-or-death cancer surgery that remained concealed from the world for a quarter of a century. Then, facing armed labor insurrection in Chicago, Cleveland demonstrated the absolute supremacy of federal law. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: A ROUGH PATCH IN THE ROOF OF THE MOUTH
On June 18, 1893, while sitting in his second-floor White House study reviewing emergency currency legislation, President Grover Cleveland ran his tongue across the roof of his mouth and felt a rough, hard ulceration. His personal physician, Dr. Robert M. O'Reilly, was summoned to examine the lesion. Looking through a dental mirror, O'Reilly saw an ominous, cauliflower-shaped sarcoma the size of a quarter growing along the left side of the President's hard palate, extending into his upper jawbone. A tissue biopsy sent secretly to the Army Medical Museum confirmed the worst: the growth was a malignant carcinoma.\n\nThe timing could not have been more catastrophic. Wall Street was crashing, banks were closing by the dozens every day, and the Treasury's gold reserve was melting away. If the public learned that the President had cancer and might die, the stock market would collapse, and vice president Adlai Stevenson—an outspoken silver supporter—would assume the presidency, destroying the gold standard. Cleveland understood the terrifying stakes. He looked at Dr. Joseph D. Bryant, his trusted surgeon, and said firmly: 'We must operate, and it must be done immediately. But not a whisper of this must ever reach the public. The country cannot bear this shock.'\n\nCleveland was acutely aware that vice presidential succession in the midst of financial collapse would trigger an immediate stock market panic and ruin foreign confidence. Vice President Stevenson's silver sympathies would have reversed the administration's fiscal strategy overnight.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GHOST SHIP IN LONG ISLAND SOUND
To ensure absolute secrecy, Dr. Bryant devised an extraordinary plan. The surgery would not take place in a hospital or at the White House, where reporters maintained 24-hour watches, but on the high seas. Cleveland's close friend, Commodore E.C. Benedict, offered his private steam yacht, the Oneida. On June 30, 1893, under the cover of darkness, Cleveland walked onto a pier in New York City, holding his four-year-old daughter Ruth, and boarded the Oneida. To journalists, the White House announced that the President was merely taking a four-day recreational fishing cruise to his summer home, Gray Gables, on Buzzards Bay in Massachusetts.\n\nWaiting aboard the Oneida was a team of six of the nation's premier surgeons, led by Dr. Bryant and Dr. William W. Keen of Philadelphia. The yacht's saloon was stripped of carpets and draperies, washed down with carbolic acid, and fitted with an operating table lashed to the mast to prevent it from sliding in rough waters. At noon on July 1, as the yacht steamed slowly through the calm waters of Long Island Sound, Cleveland was seated in a high-backed wooden armchair strapped to the mast, breathing in nitrous oxide and ether administered through a rubber funnel.\n\nThe Oneida steamed under reduced speed to minimize vibration, while Dr. Bryant and his surgical team prepared their instruments with meticulous antiseptic care. The yacht's galley was converted into an auxiliary sterilization station, boiling surgical towels and chisels in carbolic solution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: NINETY MINUTES OF SURGICAL MASTERY
What followed was a masterpiece of nineteenth-century surgical technique. Dr. Bryant understood that if he cut through Cleveland's cheek or lip, the incision would leave a visible external scar that would expose the surgery to the press. Therefore, Bryant and Keen performed the entire operation completely from inside the President's mouth, using special curved chisels, periosteal elevators, and a battery-powered galvano-cautery wire to burn away blood vessels.\n\nWorking against the gentle rocking of the waves and by the dim illumination of a porthole and kerosene lanterns, the surgeons excised the entire left upper jawbone, the hard palate, and five teeth. The cavity was packed with iodoform gauze to prevent infection. The entire ordeal lasted exactly ninety minutes, during which Cleveland lost very little blood and never regained consciousness. When the President awoke in his cabin, his face was swollen, but completely free of external scars. Five days later, a prominent New York dentist, Dr. Kasson C. Gibson, fitted Cleveland with a custom-molded vulcanized rubber denture and artificial palate. When Cleveland spoke, his gravelly, booming voice was completely unchanged. The conspiracy of silence was so total that even Vice President Stevenson and Cleveland's own cabinet were never told that the President had undergone surgery.\n\nThe surgical feat of removing an entire upper jaw without cutting facial skin was hailed by medical historians decades later as a triumph of Victorian operative surgery. The custom vulcanized rubber prosthesis restored the contour of Cleveland's face so perfectly that no casual observer could detect the loss of bone.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: E.J. EDWARDS AND THE 'LYING REPORTER'
Two months later, the secret nearly blew wide open. A brilliant, dogged investigative journalist named E.J. Edwards learned details of the operation from one of the assistant surgeons who had breached confidentiality. On August 29, 1893, Edwards published a sensational, front-page scoop in the Philadelphia Press, revealing that President Cleveland had undergone a secret operation on the yacht Oneida to remove a malignant cancer from his upper jaw.\n\nThe administration's response was swift, ruthless, and total. Cleveland's advisors and cabinet secretaries launched an aggressive smear campaign against Edwards, publicly branding him a 'disreputable liar' and a 'gutter journalist' who was inventing sensational fables to panic Wall Street. Dr. Bryant issued a deceptive public statement claiming the President had merely had two bad teeth removed. Edwards' journalistic reputation was ruined; he was ostracized by colleagues and hounded out of the Washington press corps. Cleveland went on to live another fifteen years, completely free of cancer. It was not until 1917—twenty-four years later, and nine years after Cleveland's death—that Dr. William W. Keen published a full medical account in the Saturday Evening Post, completely vindicating E.J. Edwards and confirming every single word of his 1893 scoop.\n\nE.J. Edwards suffered decades of professional hardship for printing the truth, a cautionary tale of the immense power of presidential denial against investigative journalism. Even his closest newspaper editors abandoned him in the face of the administration's fierce repudiations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: EUGENE V. DEBS AND THE PULLMAN BOYCOTT
Less than a year after his secret surgery, Cleveland faced a domestic crisis that threatened to plunge the nation into civil war. In the model company town of Pullman, Illinois, south of Chicago, railcar tycoon George M. Pullman operated a feudal corporate empire. In the wake of the Panic of 1893, Pullman slashed his workers' wages by twenty-five percent while refusing to reduce the rents on company-owned housing or the prices in company-owned grocery stores. Desperate workers went on strike in May 1894, appealing for help to the American Railway Union, led by the charismatic, radical labor organizer Eugene Victor Debs.\n\nDebs called for a nationwide boycott of all trains carrying Pullman sleeping cars. Within days, one hundred and fifty thousand railroad workers walked off the job across twenty-seven states. The entire railroad network west of Chicago was paralyzed. Freight yards were blockaded, switches were spiked, and passenger trains were halted by large, angry crowds. In Chicago, desperate mobs of unemployed drifters torched hundreds of railcars, sending massive plumes of black smoke into the sky and cutting off food supplies to eastern cities.\n\nThe Pullman strike exposed the stark, feudal reality of corporate company towns, where workers were subjected to total economic control by industrial monopolies. Families faced immediate eviction from company homes if they dared to question wage deductions or management decrees.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MAIL MUST GO THROUGH: BAYONETS IN CHICAGO
Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld, a progressive Democrat, refused to request federal troops, insisting that local police and state militia could maintain order. But Grover Cleveland took a dramatically different view. Cleveland's Attorney General, Richard Olney—a former railroad corporation attorney—obtained a sweeping federal court injunction under the Sherman Antitrust Act, declaring that the rail boycott was an illegal conspiracy in restraint of interstate commerce.\n\nCleveland seized upon a fundamental constitutional justification: the strike was obstructing the United States mail. When Governor Altgeld protested that federal intervention was unconstitutional and an invasion of states' rights, Cleveland delivered his immortal executive decree: 'If it takes the entire army and navy of the United States to deliver a postal card in Chicago, that card will be delivered!' On July 3, 1894, President Cleveland ordered twelve thousand regular United States Army soldiers, commanded by Major General Nelson A. Miles, to march into Chicago with fixed bayonets, cavalry sabers, and Gatling guns. Bloody riots erupted between soldiers and strikers, leaving thirty civilians dead and dozens wounded. But the military broke the strike; Eugene V. Debs was arrested for contempt of court and imprisoned, and rail traffic was restored across the continent.\n\nCleveland's deployment of federal troops over the fierce objections of the state governor established an enduring precedent for federal supremacy in national emergencies. The Supreme Court later upheld the injunction in In re Debs, affirming the broad inherent power of the executive branch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF IRON WILL
Grover Cleveland's actions in the Pullman Strike solidified his reputation as a leader of uncompromising, almost ruthless firmness. Conservatives praised him for maintaining law, order, and constitutional supremacy; labor unions and working-class Americans never forgave him, viewing him as a tool of corporate capital. Yet Cleveland remained serenely indifferent to both praise and condemnation. He believed that the duty of the Chief Executive was not to negotiate with lawlessness or yield to popular pressure, but to enforce the laws of the United States without hesitation.\n\nFrom the rocking saloon of the yacht Oneida to the smoke-filled rail yards of Chicago, Grover Cleveland demonstrated an iron will that was unique among nineteenth-century presidents. He was the anchor of the American state during its darkest hours of industrial transformation. In 1908, as he lay dying at his estate in Princeton, New Jersey, surrounded by his beloved wife Frances and his children, Cleveland whispered his final words to the physician who leaned over his bed: 'I have tried so hard to do right.' It was the simple, unvarnished epitaph of an immovable American president.\n\nCleveland's final years in Princeton were marked by quiet intellectual reflection, as former adversaries gradually recognized his incorruptible integrity and moral fortitude. He served as a trustee of Princeton University, maintaining his belief that honest public service required immovable adherence to principle.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Grover Cleveland's second term remains a masterclass in executive resolve. By bearing personal agony in silence and standing firm against civil unrest, he preserved the stability of the American Republic. Next week, we turn our attention to the dawn of the twentieth century and the presidency of William McKinley—the Front Porch Campaign of 1896, the Spanish-American War, and the tragic assassination in Buffalo that thrust Theodore Roosevelt into the White House. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
